title: Universities Urge DHS to Withdraw $70,000 OPT Fee as Comment Period Closes
excerpt: The American Council on Education and 36 other higher-education groups filed on the final day of public comments, arguing the per-student fee would deepen enrollment declines and could worsen the fraud it is meant to curb.
body:
• Under the DHS proposal published on October 8, a college would pay $70,000 before recommending an F-1 student for initial OPT, plus $30,000 for each later recommendation, including a STEM OPT extension — up to $100,000 per student.
  • The American Council on Education (ACE) and 36 other higher-education associations used the final day of the public comment period, November 9, to urge DHS to withdraw the proposal in its entirety.
  • Nothing has changed yet: this is a proposed rule, not a final one, and current OPT rules and fees remain in effect, according to Yale's Office of International Students and Scholars.
  • If you are an F-1 student, your next step is unchanged — work through your university's Designated School Official (DSO); no new fee is due unless a final rule is published, and any final fee would take effect 60 days after publication.

The American Council on Education and 36 other higher-education associations have urged the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw its proposed Optional Practical Training (OPT) fee in its entirety, in a comment letter filed on Monday, the final day of the public comment period. The fee is the centerpiece of a proposed rule, published on October 8 under docket ICEB-2026-0100, that would charge colleges and universities $70,000 for each initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each subsequent one.

Who is affected, exactly

OPT lets eligible F-1 students work in a job related to their field of study, generally for up to 12 months, with a further 24-month extension available to qualifying STEM graduates. The proposed charge falls not on the student but on the SEVP-certified school, which must pay it to the Treasury Department before it can recommend a student at all. According to ACE, the money would not go to DHS and would not be used for processing, fraud investigations or enforcement. Students currently pay $520 to apply for work authorization. DHS has said schools could pass the cost on to F-1 students, to all students, or to employers.

That pass-through is the practical issue for Indian students, who make up one of the largest international cohorts in the United States. A university that cannot absorb $70,000 per recommendation has three options, each of which lands on students: raise the cost for international students, spread it across all tuition, or stop recommending OPT.

What each side says

DHS says the fees are meant to curb fraud and protect American workers. The higher-education groups answer that a price is the wrong test of integrity. Their letter argues the fee amounts to a pay-to-play system that, in their words, "does not help distinguish between a responsible institution and a qualified student and appears to punish institutions that follow the rules." They warn it could push students toward unregulated employment arrangements and predatory third-party financing, and they propose alternatives instead: risk-based audits, employer-side verification, site visits, and a fee calibrated to the actual cost of oversight. NAFSA, the international educators' association, made the same withdrawal request in its own comment letter dated November 3, which can be read in full here.

The enrollment backdrop

The letter cites a 17% decline in new international enrollment in 2025-26, according to the Institute of International Education, with some institutions projecting drops of 40% to 60%. It also cites a NAFSA estimate that international students contribute more than $40 billion a year to the US economy and support more than 368,000 domestic jobs, and a 2018 Business Roundtable analysis concluding that a 60% reduction in OPT participation would cost 443,000 jobs over a decade. The groups add that the fee would stack on top of a separate DHS effort to end "duration of status" for students, which is currently blocked by a court order the administration is appealing.

What happens next

DHS must consider the comments it received before it can publish a final rule, and it may change or drop the proposal. Yale's international office notes that it is not known if or when a final rule will be published, or whether it will differ from the proposal. If a final rule is issued, the fees would take effect 60 days after publication. Until then, OPT works as before: students apply through their school as usual, and no $70,000 payment is due from anyone.
